beats.narration_text: Someone wondered: can Claude clear a new product of patent risk? No — clearing is a legal opinion, and this skill won't produce one. Here's what actually happens when you run it: Claude loads a fixed triage checklist, screens your product description against it, and flags what needs a closer look. Screening, not clearance. Different job.

beats.narration_text: A skill is a folder Claude reads before it works. This one is called fto-triage — one folder, one file: SKILL.md. That file holds the entire instruction set in plain language. No hidden logic, no compiled step, no baked-in behavior. Claude reads it, then acts on what it says. The file is the program — which means to change what Claude does, you change the file, not the model.

props.title: A skill is a folder.
props.calloutText: The SKILL.md is the instruction set.

beats.narration_text: The pipeline lives in the Steps section. Claude reads each step in order and runs it — no branching, no re-ordering, no clever shortcuts, unless a step explicitly says so. That linearity is a design choice, and it costs flexibility. What you get back for that cost is repeatability: same request in, same shape of report out.

Here's what's actually happening inside a step. Screen the described product or feature against the claim elements, keywords, and jurisdictions the file specifies — flag anything that matches, and stop. That's it. Stay inside that checklist and the report holds its shape every time. This is the trade-off the skill makes on purpose: it gives up creative reasoning in exchange for repeatability. It works if you value a first-pass screen you can hand to a lawyer; it fails if you were hoping the model would decide.

beats.narration_text: Same checklist in, same triage report out, every time. That's what this skill does. Deciding whether you're actually clear to operate — that's a legal call, and the skill doesn't make legal calls. It hands you a first-pass screen. You still take it to a lawyer.

props.quote: Same checklist in, same triage report out, every time. The clearance call is still yours.
props.sparkLine: Screening, not clearance — the deciding is still yours.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste straight into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — read it with me. I'm about to ship a new product feature; here's a short description of what it does. Act as a freedom-to-operate triage — not a clearance opinion. Tell me exactly what you need from me before you run any screen — jurisdiction, target markets, prior-art categories to check against. Walk me through the specific claim elements and keywords you'd screen for, then flag anything that matches and tell me what a real patent attorney would need to see before giving an actual clearance opinion. That last clause is the whole point of the exercise — a flag is a question you still have to answer with a person. Go deeper: for a triage that flags nothing, what is the smallest change to your product description that would flip a flag on — and what does that tell you about how much your clearance actually depends on how you describe what you built? Liam, in for Bear.

(2) Walk me through the specific claim elements and keywords you'd screen the description against. (3) Flag anything that matches, and for each flag, tell me exactly what a real patent attorney would need to see before giving an actual clearance opinion.
